source_batch.unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) and other Remittance Facilities for Residents

facts.statement: Under section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (in force from 1 April 2026), an authorised dealer collects tax at source on a remittance under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme of an amount or aggregate of amounts exceeding ten lakh rupees: at 2% where the purpose is education or medical treatment and at 20% for other purposes.

The authorised dealer does not collect tax on an LRS remittance that is a loan obtained from a financial institution for the purpose of pursuing education, nor on an amount on which the seller has already collected tax on an overseas tour programme package, nor where the buyer is liable to deduct tax at source under another provision and has deducted it.

The sale of an overseas tour programme package, including travel, hotel stay, boarding or lodging and similar expenses, attracts tax collected by the seller at 2%. The Finance Bill 2026 memorandum proposed that the threshold for this provision be removed so that it applies irrespective of the amount.
facts.locator: Section 394(1), Table, item 8; Finance Bill 2026 memorandum, paragraph 8 on Table item 8

facts.statement: Before 1 April 2026 the rate for LRS remittances for education or medical treatment above ten lakh rupees was 5%; the Finance Bill 2026 proposed reducing it to 2%. The courseware (S03 printed pp. 53-54) describes the rules of 1 October 2020: 5% above Rs 7 lakh, 0.5% for an education loan, 10% without PAN.
facts.locator: Paragraph 6 on Table item 7; S03 printed pp. 53-54

payload.title: TCS on foreign remittances: the three things to know
payload.core_explanation_md:
When a resident individual sends money abroad under the LRS, the **authorised dealer bank collects tax at source (TCS)** from the remitter. Three facts decide it.

1. **The trigger**: the remittances in the financial year, taken together, **exceed ₹10 lakh**.
2. **The rate depends on the purpose**: **2%** for **education or medical treatment**; **20%** for **every other purpose** (investment abroad, gifts, family maintenance, travel and the rest).
3. **The collector**: the authorised dealer bank, at the time of the remittance.

The provision is section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026.

payload.title: When no TCS is collected on an LRS remittance
payload.core_explanation_md:
Three situations switch the collection off or move it to someone else.

- **Education funded by a loan** from a financial institution: **no TCS** on that remittance.
- **Overseas tour package**: the **seller** (the tour operator) collects **2%** on the package price, with no ₹10 lakh threshold. The bank does **not** collect again on the amount the seller has already taxed.
- **Tax already deducted**: if the person receiving the money is subject to tax deducted at source under another provision of the Act and it **has** been deducted, the bank does not collect TCS.

Check order for a bank officer: *tour package already taxed? education loan? tax already deducted? If none, test the ₹10 lakh aggregate.*

payload.title: TCS across a year of remittances for investment abroad
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case, taxed at the rate for purposes other than education or medical treatment (20%): a resident individual remits ₹4,00,000 in May, ₹8,50,000 in August and ₹1,00,000 in December, all to buy investments abroad. Tax is collected on the part of the year's total above the ₹10 lakh threshold. How much TCS is collected on each remittance?

worked_steps.description: May: running total is ₹4,00,000, below the threshold.
August: running total after the remittance.
The part of the total above the threshold is taxed at 20%.
December: the whole ₹1,00,000 falls above the threshold, so it is all taxed at 20%.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: TCS: ₹0.00 in May, ₹50,000.00 in August and ₹20,000.00 in December, ₹70,000.00 in all

self_check.prompt_text: Had all three remittances been for education paid from the remitter's own funds, what would the August and December TCS have been?

payload.title: Old numbers in older books: what changed in 2026
payload.core_explanation_md:
Courseware written in 2020 or soon after teaches the **original** TCS rules: **5%** on LRS remittances above **₹7 lakh**, **0.5%** for an education loan, and **10%** if PAN or Aadhaar is missing.

The current position for the December 2026 exam (section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025):

- Threshold: **₹10 lakh** a year, not ₹7 lakh.
- Education or medical treatment: **2%** (it was 5% until 1 April 2026).
- All other purposes: **20%**.
- Education loan from a financial institution: **no TCS** (not 0.5%).
- Overseas tour package: **2%** collected by the seller, with no threshold.

If an exam question quotes the older figures, it follows the older rules; the table above is the current law.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of these figures is out of date: ₹7 lakh threshold, ₹10 lakh threshold, 2% for education, 20% for investment?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The ₹7 lakh threshold. The current threshold is ₹10 lakh.

unresolved: The Income-tax Act, 2025 text retrieved says "an amount or aggregate of the amounts exceeding ten lakh rupees" without spelling out whether the rate applies to the excess only. The items compute on the part above the threshold, which is how the courseware examples (printed pp. 53-54) and the earlier provision worked and how the Finance Bill memorandum describes it, but explicit current wording was not retrieved. The stems state the basis.

The footnote to section 394 quotes an earlier form of the table clauses ("5% of amount or aggregate of amounts up to ten lakh rupees; 20% of amount or aggregate of amounts exceeding ten lakh rupees"), whose reading is unclear; the current clauses are used.
Whether the aggregate for the threshold mixes purposes (education and other) is not stated in the text retrieved; no item mixes purposes in one computation.
The additional 10% rate where PAN or Aadhaar is not furnished (courseware) is not taught: it belongs to a separate section not retrieved.
TCS on transfers from a domestic rupee account to an NRO account under the LRS (courseware printed p. 53) is not taught.
Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 4 of 2026) is cited through the Income Tax Department's section 394 page and its footnotes; the Act itself was not downloaded.
